lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- Running Your Part of the Meeting
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Amanda Merlini | Lesson 3 -- Running Your Part of the Meeting

vocab.title: Match each expression to its meaning
defs: to be responsible for work that other people do
to come back to something later and check that it moved
the list of points a meeting will cover, in order
to say out loud that something worries you, before it becomes a problem
to close a meeting or a subject with a short summary
one task the meeting produced, with an owner and a date
to keep regular contact with another team so that both know what the other is doing
the written record of what a meeting decided

items.situation: It is your turn on the agenda. Open your item.
tips: Thanks. On item three, we have been reviewing the supply contracts since Monday.
Open with the item number, then the status. Never with an apology.

items.situation: Paul asks: "What has legal been doing about the delayed shipment?"
tips: We have been talking to the buyer every day this week, and we have not sent a formal notice yet.
The work in progress takes have been + ing.

items.situation: Somebody is going too far off the point and the meeting has ten minutes left.
tips: Can we come back to that after the agenda? I would like to close item three first.
Hold the thread without shutting the person down.

items.situation: You disagree with a deadline that the commercial team just proposed.
tips: I would like to raise a concern about the date. Two weeks is not enough for the legal review.
Name it as a concern, give the reason, then propose.

items.situation: The meeting is over and nobody has written anything down.
tips: Let me wrap up. Three action items: I send the draft on Thursday, Paul confirms the volume, and we meet again on Monday.
Wrap up means: who does what, by when.

items.situation: A colleague asks what you do on a normal week, not this week.
tips: I oversee the legal department, and I liaise with the commercial team every day.
Permanent responsibility takes the present simple, not the continuous.

listenings.text: Hi Amanda, it is Clara. Two changes to the alignment meeting on Wednesday. First, it moves from four o'clock to two, because the commercial director is flying out that evening. Second, the agenda is shorter. We have cut the pricing review, so there are three items only: the delayed shipment, the new supply contract, and the training on the compliance policy. You own item three, and you have ten minutes for it. One more thing, and this is the part people forget. Nobody has been taking minutes since March, so last month we repeated two decisions that were already made. I am asking each owner to write down the action items for their own item and send them to me the same day. Thank you, Amanda.

Amanda, it is Paul. I am recording this before Wednesday so that we do not spend the meeting catching up. Here is where we are. We have been negotiating with the new buyer for three weeks, and we are close, but they have been asking for a shorter payment term every single round. On the delayed shipment, the vessel has been waiting at the port since Friday and the cost is growing every day. My team has been calling the agent twice a day and getting nothing. What I need from you on Wednesday is not a legal opinion, it is a decision: do we send the formal notice now, or do we wait one more week? Bring both options and tell me what the risk is on each. See you Wednesday.

extra_audio.text: Open your item and say where things stand. Then give the one fact that everybody needs. Then raise the concern, with the reason behind it. Then propose what you want the meeting to decide. And finally, close with the action items: who does what, by when.
